# Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series

CCS: Computing methodologies Machine learningCCS: Information
systems Data miningCCS: Computing methodologies Anomaly detection

David Berghaus Affiliation: Lamarr Institute, Germany
Affiliation: Fraunhofer IAIS, Germany email:
<david.berghaus@iais.fraunhofer.de>

###### Abstract.

Time-series anomaly detection trades off predictive accuracy,
computational efficiency, and interpretability. We use a large language
model not as the detector but as the _author_ of one: an autonomous
research loop in which the model repeatedly edits a single short NumPy
program under a leakage-free objective, keeping the best-scoring
detector it finds. The loop discovers two compact detectors, one for
univariate and one for multivariate series, that describe short windows
by their local spectral features and compare them with the
training-region distribution through a covariance-aware distance. On the
TSB-AD benchmark these detectors lead the field across metrics, ahead of
the strongest classical, deep, and foundation-model baselines including
Time-RCD, yet they train no network and use no GPU, and the multivariate
detector is faster than every similarly performing baseline. LLM-driven
program search is thus a practical route to accurate, efficient, and
transparent detectors.

###### Keywords: 

time series anomaly detection, automated algorithm discovery, LLM-driven
program search, interpretable models

## 1. Introduction

Anomaly detection in time series underpins a long list of practical
systems, from monitoring industrial machinery and spacecraft telemetry
to flagging irregular heartbeats and intrusions in network traffic.
Despite sustained attention, the field has not converged on a clear
winner. In multivariate settings, deep models can be more competitive,
especially when cross-channel structure matters, but strong classical
methods such as KMeans and KNN remain among the leading baselines ([Qiu
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib6); [Liu and Paparrizos, 2024](#bib.bib7)). No
single method dominates across datasets, anomaly types, and
computational budgets.

Classical detectors are cheap and simple but often require
dataset-specific preprocessing and threshold tuning to perform well.
Deep and foundation models reduce the manual tuning burden but pay for
it with training cost, GPU dependence, and opacity.

We take a different angle: rather than designing a detector by hand or
training a large model, we use an _LLM-driven autonomous research loop_
as a tool to write the detector for us. A language model repeatedly
edits a single short Python and NumPy program. It is given the benchmark
harness, a strict leakage-free protocol, and an instruction to find an
accurate, elegant, single-principle detector. Each edited program is run
through the harness and scored on a held-out validation split; this
score, together with the whole trajectory of past attempts (including
edits that lowered it), informs the next edit.

Using a language model as an engine for proposing and refining programs,
rather than as the final model, underlies a growing line of work in
mathematical and algorithmic discovery ([Romera-Paredes et al.,
2024](#bib.bib3); [Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Lange et al.,
2025](#bib.bib4); [Berghaus, 2026](#bib.bib5)). Our question is a
practical one: is this tool effective for time-series anomaly detection,
and what kind of detector does it produce? As ablations we also hold the
harness, the seed program (a simple z-score detector), and the
single-principle prompt _fixed_ and vary the search by driving the loop
with other models (GPT 5.6 Terra and the smaller open MiniMax-2.5) and
comparing against an off-the-shelf evolutionary program-search
framework, ShinkaEvolve ([Lange et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)), which is an
open-source alternative to AlphaEvolve ([Novikov et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2)).

The search does not require existing labels: candidates are scored
against synthetic anomalies injected into a slice of the training data,
never against real labels, so the approach is also applicable to
real-world problems where no ground truth exists. At inference the
discovered detector is fit per series without labels, under the same
operating assumptions as a classical unsupervised detector such as
KMeans. We steer the search toward short, efficient programs, and run it
separately for univariate and multivariate series.

Our contributions are as follows.

- •
  An LLM that writes the detector. We show that an LLM-driven autonomous
  research loop is an effective tool for discovering anomaly detectors.
  The search is straightforward to set up, demands little
  anomaly-detection expertise from the practitioner, and produces a
  detector that is compact, interpretable, and competitive with the
  state of the art. Each detector emerged from a single one hour session
  of roughly $`100`$ edit-and-evaluate iterations.
- •
  Interpretable, single-CPU programs. Each detector is a short NumPy
  program with no GPU, no neural training, and no learned weights, so
  its inductive biases can be read directly from the source and audited.
- •
  Field-leading accuracy. On the established TSB-AD benchmark the two
  detectors take the most first-place finishes on every reported metric
  across both regimes, ahead of classical baselines as well as deep and
  pretrained detectors including the Time-RCD foundation model ([Lan et
  al., 2026](#bib.bib47))
  (Table [2](#S6.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Corroboration on TAB ‣ 6.1. Accuracy on TSB-AD ‣ 6. Results ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")),
  and also perform competitively on the recent TAB benchmark
  (Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Complete result tables ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")).

## 2. Related work

#### Benchmarks and evaluation for time series anomaly detection

Our primary benchmark is TSB-AD ([Liu and Paparrizos, 2024](#bib.bib7)),
which we evaluate under the 16-family protocol published with
Time-RCD ([Lan et al., 2026](#bib.bib47)). On TSB-AD we compare against
detectors spanning pretrained, deep, and classical families: the recent
Time-RCD foundation model ([Lan et al., 2026](#bib.bib47)); the deep
reconstruction and forecasting detectors TranAD ([Tuli et al.,
2022](#bib.bib32)), USAD ([Audibert et al., 2020](#bib.bib31)),
OmniAnomaly ([Su et al., 2019](#bib.bib30)), and DCdetector ([Yang et
al., 2023](#bib.bib33)), together with the temporal-frequency masked
autoencoder TFMAE ([Fang et al., 2024](#bib.bib34)); and the classical
baselines LOF ([Breunig et al., 2000](#bib.bib22)), Isolation
Forest ([Liu et al., 2008](#bib.bib11)), and subsequence PCA ([Shyu et
al., 2003](#bib.bib12)). For a broader picture we additionally report
results on the more recent TAB benchmark ([Qiu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib6)) in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Complete result tables ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series").

#### Autonomous research agents and LLM-driven discovery

A growing body of work uses large language models not as the final model
but as an engine for proposing and refining code. FunSearch showed that
searching over LLM-proposed programs can yield new results in
mathematics ([Romera-Paredes et al., 2024](#bib.bib3)); AlphaEvolve
broadened this into a general coding agent for scientific and
algorithmic discovery ([Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)); and open
frameworks such as ShinkaEvolve study how to make such program search
sample-efficient ([Lange et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)). Most directly,
[Karpathy (2026)](#bib.bib1) articulates the idea of an
autonomous-research loop in a CLI in which an LLM agent repeatedly
proposes an edit to a single artifact, evaluates it against a fixed
metric, and iterates without human intervention. Closest in application,
EVIL evolves compact, interpretable algorithms for zero-shot inference
on event sequences and time series ([Berghaus, 2026](#bib.bib5)). This
program-authoring role is distinct from using a language model _as_ the
time-series model: One-Fits-All repurposes a frozen pretrained
language-model backbone for downstream tasks including anomaly
detection ([Zhou et al., 2023](#bib.bib38)), and time-series foundation
models score data directly from learned weights ([Lan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib47)). In our setting the language model never sees the
data at inference; it only writes the detector program, and the object
that scores each series is a few lines of NumPy.

#### Synthetic data for foundation models

Synthetic simulation is increasingly used to pretrain foundation models
for time series and event sequences, where it supplies a broad prior
over mechanisms that can be adapted or applied zero-shot to real data.
Related time-series foundation-model work uses synthetic anomalies and
relative contexts (Time-RCD), causally coherent kernel-generated series
(CauKer), or synthetic series paired with symbolic expressions
(SymTime) ([Lan et al., 2026](#bib.bib47); [Xie et al.,
2026](#bib.bib48); [Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib49)).

## 3. Discovering detectors with an autonomous research loop

#### Detector representation

Each candidate detector is a self-contained Python and NumPy function
with a fixed signature: it consumes a training segment and a test
segment of a series and returns a per-timestep anomaly score.
Restricting candidates to short array programs has two benefits. The
programs are cheap to run, so a single evaluation across the validation
set takes minutes rather than hours, which is what makes an iterative
loop practical; and they remain interpretable, so the design choices
that perform well can be read directly from the code.

#### The loop

We use an autonomous research loop similar to ([Karpathy,
2026](#bib.bib1)): an LLM-driven agent that edits and re-evaluates a
single program with no human intervention. A fixed harness defines the
data interface, the validation objective, and the scoring code. The
language model is allowed to edit only the detector program. In each
iteration it (i) inspects the current detector program and its recent
scores, (ii) proposes a concrete modification, ranging from a
hyperparameter change to a new scoring component or a structural
rewrite, (iii) runs the modified program through the harness on the
validation split, and (iv) reads the resulting validation score. Unlike
a hill-climbing search, the loop applies no automatic accept/reject
step: the full trajectory of attempts, including edits that lower the
score, stays in the agent’s context and serves as inspiration for later
proposals, and the single program returned by the search is the
best-scoring one over the whole session (formalized below). We steer the
loop toward short, single-principle programs rather than accuracy alone,
which keeps the discovered detectors readable instead of letting them
grow into opaque ensembles. We run each search independently for the
univariate and multivariate settings and with several driving models
(Section [5](#S5 "5. Experimental setup ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")).
The strongest loop, driven by Opus 4.8, discovers related
spectral-Gaussian novelty patterns in the two regimes, whereas the other
loops and the evolutionary baseline arrive at different programs
(Section [6.4](#S6.SS4 "6.4. Ablation: the model and the search procedure ‣ 6. Results ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")).

#### Synthetic validation and leakage control

The search uses _no real anomaly labels_. Candidates are scored by
detecting synthetic anomalies injected only into a held-out slice of
each series’ _training_ region. The generator is an explicit prior over
what an anomaly can look like. We aim for anomalies that are realistic
in the mechanism that produces them, like a sensor that freezes, a valid
shape appearing out of context, a cycle at the wrong period or phase.
Its types are taken from the established GutenTAG taxonomy ([Wenig et
al., 2022](#bib.bib8)), and its mix spans both the magnitude and the
in-range shape/contextual families, so that a candidate cannot score
well by handling only one of them. The univariate mix emphasizes the
in-range families, which cannot be caught from magnitude alone, while
the multivariate mix also includes joint cross-channel perturbations.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Search configuration ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")
gives the complete generator and leakage-control protocol.

## 4. Methods discovered by the searches

Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4. Methods discovered by the searches ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")
summarizes the programs selected by all four searches. The strongest
search, the Opus 4.8 loop, found two spectral-Gaussian novelty methods
and performed best overall; we therefore describe those two methods
below. The other loops produced simpler local-feature methods, while the
Shinka evolutions produced ensembles of standard signals. The
evaluations can be found in
Section [6](#S6 "6. Results ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series");
constants and complete executable implementations of the Opus methods
are in
Appendices [C](#A3 "Appendix C Discovered detector configurations ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")
and [D](#A4 "Appendix D Discovered algorithms ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series").
The complete, runnable source code of every discovered detector (all
four searches, in both the univariate and multivariate regimes) is

| Search                   | Univariate method                                                           | Multivariate method                                                               |

Table 1. Methods selected by each search. Entries summarize the final
program in each regime; full accuracy results appear in
Section [6](#S6 "6. Results ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series").

#### The Opus methods

The Opus loop was run once for each regime, and both times it arrived at
a detector built on the same idea. Each one slides a short window along
the series, describes the rhythms inside that window, and then asks how
unusual that description looks next to normal stretches of the training
data. Windows that stand out get a high anomaly score, which is turned
back into a per-timestamp score. Both detectors are fast, with a running
time that grows roughly in proportion to the length of the series. Where
they differ is the description they use: the univariate detector
captures how a window’s energy is spread across its rhythms, while the
multivariate detector captures the combined rhythms of all channels at
once.

#### The univariate detector

Rather than looking at the raw values in a window, this detector looks
at how the window’s energy is split between fast and slow rhythms, and
at the overall shape of that split. It turns each window into a short
list of descriptive numbers, for example how peaked or how flat the
spectrum is, where its energy sits, and how much of it falls in slow
versus fast rhythms, together with a term that reacts when part of the
window suddenly goes quiet or freezes. Earlier frequency-based detectors
compare a spectrum against a smoothed baseline ([Ren et al.,
2019](#bib.bib41)), score windows by their distance to a nearest
neighbour ([Yeh et al., 2016](#bib.bib20)), or learn a frequency-domain
reconstruction ([Fang et al., 2024](#bib.bib34); [Xu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib39)); what is different here is that the description is
fixed, easy to read, and judged as a whole rather than one number at a
time. The score therefore rises not just when a single number is
unusual, but when the normal relationship between them breaks. Because
the description is mostly about shape and rhythm rather than the raw
size of the values, the detector also catches anomalies whose values
stay in the normal range and that value-based detectors tend to miss,
such as cycles running at the wrong period or phase, out-of-context
subsequences, and frozen segments. It repeats this at several window
sizes and blends the results, giving extra weight to the windows that
look genuinely improbable. To our knowledge this particular construction
has not previously been used for anomaly detection, and we verify
empirically that it outperforms the closest existing frequency-domain
and feature-based detectors
(Section [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2. Did the loop rediscover an existing detector? ‣ 6. Results ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")).

Formally, a window $`x\in\mathbb{R}^{w}`$ is Hann-tapered and
mean-removed, $`u=(x-\bar{x})\odot h`$, with power spectrum
$`P_{k}=|\mathrm{FFT}(u)_{k}|^{2}`$, $`k=1,\dots,m`$
($`m=\lfloor w/2\rfloor`$), normalized to $`p_{k}=P_{k}/\sum_{j}P_{j}`$
($`\hat{\sigma}`$ a standard deviation, $`\delta`$ a small constant).
Its spectral-organization signature stacks eight scalars,

|     |     |                              |                                                                                                       |                                  |                                                                                 |     |
| --- | --- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- |
| (1) |     | $`\displaystyle H`$          | $`\displaystyle=-\textstyle\sum_{k}p_{k}\log p_{k},`$                                                 | $`\displaystyle\kappa`$          | $`\displaystyle=\max\nolimits_{k}p_{k},`$                                       |     |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle c`$          | $`\displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{k}k\,p_{k},`$                                                         | $`\displaystyle\varepsilon_{E}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\log(\hat{\sigma}_{x}+\delta),`$                                |     |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{SF}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\log\tfrac{(\prod_{k}P_{k})^{1/m}}{m^{-1}\sum_{k}P_{k}},`$                            | $`\displaystyle\rho`$            | $`\displaystyle=\log\tfrac{\sum_{k\leq m/2}P_{k}}{\sum_{k>m/2}P_{k}},`$         |     |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle\beta`$       | $`\displaystyle=\tfrac{\sum_{k}(\ell_{k}-\bar{\ell})\log P_{k}}{\sum_{k}(\ell_{k}-\bar{\ell})^{2}},`$ | $`\displaystyle\gamma`$          | $`\displaystyle=\log\tfrac{\min_{b}\hat{\sigma}_{x^{[b]}}}{\hat{\sigma}_{x}},`$ |     |

namely the entropy $`H`$, peak concentration $`\kappa`$, centroid $`c`$,
log-energy $`\varepsilon_{E}`$, log flatness $`\mathrm{SF}`$, low/high
band ratio $`\rho`$, log–log spectral slope $`\beta`$
($`\ell_{k}=\log k`$), and a complexity-collapse term $`\gamma`$ over
four sub-blocks $`x^{[b]}`$. Appending a bank of $`N=11`$ log-spaced
band-powers
$`\phi_{\mathrm{band},b}=\log(\sum_{k\in\mathcal{B}_{b}}p_{k}+\delta)`$
gives the descriptor $`\phi(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{19}`$. This descriptor is
scored by a shrunk full-covariance Mahalanobis distance to the Gaussian
of normal windows and fused across a dyadic scale space with a
tail-emphasized weighting. The exact score and fusion, and all
constants, are given in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Discovered detector configurations ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")
(Eqs. [3](#A3.E3 "In Univariate detector ‣ Appendix C Discovered detector configurations ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")–[4](#A3.E4 "In Univariate detector ‣ Appendix C Discovered detector configurations ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")).

#### The multivariate detector

For series with many channels, the detector describes the rhythms of all
channels together. It slides a window across the channels, removes each
window’s level so that only its shape matters, and measures how much
energy each channel carries in a few frequency bands. Stacking these
across all channels gives one description of the window’s joint rhythm.
It then builds a single statistical model of what normal windows look
like and scores each window by how far it lies from that model. Because
all channels share one model, the score reacts not only when a single
channel’s rhythm changes, but when the usual relationship between the
channels breaks, even if every channel on its own still looks perfectly
normal. To stay fast, the detector samples windows at regular strides
and caps how many it uses, so its cost grows roughly in proportion to
the length of the series even for very long, high-dimensional data. And
because the model has a fixed size rather than growing with the data,
one fit on a short training segment carries over to much longer test
series. The full description and all constants are given in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Discovered detector configurations ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")
(Eqs. [5](#A3.E5 "In Multivariate detector ‣ Appendix C Discovered detector configurations ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")–[6](#A3.E6 "In Multivariate detector ‣ Appendix C Discovered detector configurations ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")).

## 5. Experimental setup

#### Benchmarks and datasets

Our primary evaluation is the established TSB-AD ([Liu and Paparrizos,
2024](#bib.bib7)), using the 16-family protocol of Time-RCD ([Lan et
al., 2026](#bib.bib47)): eleven univariate families (IOPS, MGAB, NAB,
NEK, Power, SED, Stock, TODS, UCR, WSD, Yahoo) and five multivariate
families (MSL, PSM, SMAP, SMD, SWaT), all listed in
Table [2](#S6.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Corroboration on TAB ‣ 6.1. Accuracy on TSB-AD ‣ 6. Results ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series").
For completeness we additionally evaluate on TAB ([Qiu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib6)), a more recent benchmark that assembles a larger and
differently curated field, both univariate ($`14`$ dataset families,
$`816`$ series) and multivariate ($`25`$ families, $`214`$ series),
under a single evaluation pipeline and reports a wider panel of range-
and volume-aware metrics. We report its full fields in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Complete result tables ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series").

#### Metrics

On TSB-AD we follow the Time-RCD protocol and report the affiliation
F-measure ([Huet et al., 2022](#bib.bib10)), a tolerance-aware temporal
F1 (F1-T), the point-wise standard F1, and VUS-PR ([Paparrizos et al.,
2022](#bib.bib9)). On TAB we report the panel it standardizes: the
volume-under-the-surface pair (VUS-PR, VUS-ROC), the two range-aware
areas under the curve (R-AUC-PR, R-AUC-ROC) ([Paparrizos et al.,
2022](#bib.bib9)), and the affiliation F-measure ([Huet et al.,
2022](#bib.bib10)). Precise definitions are in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Metric definitions ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series").

#### Baselines and protocol

On TSB-AD we adopt the published 16-family protocol of Time-RCD ([Lan et
al., 2026](#bib.bib47)) and place our detectors, scored under that
protocol, against the baseline results reported for it: the Time-RCD
foundation model ([Lan et al., 2026](#bib.bib47)), the deep detectors
TranAD ([Tuli et al., 2022](#bib.bib32)), USAD ([Audibert et al.,
2020](#bib.bib31)), OmniAnomaly ([Su et al., 2019](#bib.bib30)),
DCdetector ([Yang et al., 2023](#bib.bib33)), and TFMAE ([Fang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib34)), and the classical baselines LOF ([Breunig et al.,
2000](#bib.bib22)), Isolation Forest ([Liu et al., 2008](#bib.bib11)),
and subsequence PCA ([Shyu et al., 2003](#bib.bib12)). Time-RCD is the
strongest non-classical baseline in this field. On TAB
(Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Complete result tables ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series"))
we compare against the full field of detectors bundled with the
benchmark, spanning non-learning, classical, and deep methods (for
example HBOS ([Goldstein and Dengel, 2012](#bib.bib13)), EIF ([Hariri et
al., 2021](#bib.bib21)), KMeans, DWT-MLEAD ([Thill et al.,
2017](#bib.bib46)), and deep models such as TimesNet ([Wu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib14)), ModernTCN ([Luo and Wang, 2024](#bib.bib16)),
PatchTST ([Nie et al., 2023](#bib.bib17)), iTransformer ([Liu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib18)), CATCH ([Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)), DUET ([Qiu et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib36)), and the Anomaly Transformer ([Xu et al.,
2022](#bib.bib15))), together with the foundation models Time-RCD ([Lan
et al., 2026](#bib.bib47)), TSPulse ([Ekambaram et al.,
2026](#bib.bib50)), and Chronos ([Ansari et al., 2024](#bib.bib51)) (the
last scored by its one-step forecast residuals, univariate only), all
run from their released checkpoints without tuning. We verified that our
evaluation scripts reproduced the numbers reported in the paper,
confirming the wrappers are faithful and that the comparison is
one-to-one.

#### The searches we compare

As ablations we ask how much the discovered detector depends on the
driving model and on the search procedure, rather than on the harness
alone. We compare four searches that hold the harness, the seed program,
the synthetic-validation objective, and the single-principle prompt
_fixed_, varying only the model and the search procedure. Three are
instances of the agentic loop above, driven by various language models
(Claude Opus 4.8, GPT 5.6 Terra, and the smaller open MiniMax-2.5), each
run at the model’s _default_ reasoning-effort setting for a single
one-hour session of roughly $`100`$ evolutions per regime. The fourth
swaps the agentic loop for ShinkaEvolve ([Lange et al.,
2025](#bib.bib4)), an off-the-shelf evolutionary program-search
framework (island populations with an elite archive) in the style of
AlphaEvolve ([Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)), driven by the same open
MiniMax-2.5 model for a matched budget of $`100`$ generations per
regime. For every search we select the program with the best
synthetic-validation score and evaluate it on both benchmarks exactly as
we evaluate the baselines.

### 6.1. Accuracy on TSB-AD

Table [2](#S6.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Corroboration on TAB ‣ 6.1. Accuracy on TSB-AD ‣ 6. Results ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")
reports accuracy on TSB-AD under the Time-RCD protocol, across the
eleven univariate and five multivariate dataset families and the four
protocol metrics (affiliation F-measure, temporal F1-T, standard F1, and
VUS-PR). The _Opus 4.8 Loop_ row applies the univariate detector to the
univariate families and the multivariate detector to the multivariate
families; within each metric the best value per family is marked with a
podium medal
(![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
for first, second, and third), and the final three columns count how
often each method places first, second, or third across the sixteen
families.

#### The Opus loop leads the field

The detector discovered by the Opus 4.8 loop takes the most first-place
finishes on every one of the four metrics, and its advantage is widest
on the precision-oriented metrics (standard F1 and VUS-PR). Its closest
competitor is Time-RCD, a foundation model pretrained for zero-shot
anomaly detection. The remaining deep detectors and the classical
baselines trail further back and top only isolated families. Among our
own searches the one exception is the multivariate side of TSB-AD, where
the GPT 5.6 Terra loop’s detector is marginally ahead of the Opus one
(Section [6.4](#S6.SS4 "6.4. Ablation: the model and the search procedure ‣ 6. Results ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series"),
Table [7](#A5.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Appendix E Complete result tables ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")).
The Opus detector remains clearly in front on the univariate families
and on both halves of TAB
(Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Complete result tables ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series"),
Tables [5](#A5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Appendix E Complete result tables ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")
and [6](#A5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix E Complete result tables ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")).

Figure 2. Qualitative score comparison on four representative TAB
univariate held-out test suffixes: two point anomalies (left) and two
contextual anomalies (right). Each column shows the observed signal and
the scores from the Opus Loop’s discovered detector, Time-RCD ([Lan et
al., 2026](#bib.bib47)), HBOS ([Goldstein and Dengel,
2012](#bib.bib13)), and Isolation Forest ([Liu et al.,
2008](#bib.bib11)); orange bands mark the labeled anomaly range. The
Opus Loop produces a sustained high score over each labeled event, while
the comparators either miss the event or also respond strongly to normal
cycles. For display, each score trace is independently normalized to
$`[0,1]`$, preserving its within-series ordering.

#### Corroboration on TAB

The larger TAB field
(Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Complete result tables ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series"),
Tables [5](#A5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Appendix E Complete result tables ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")
and [6](#A5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix E Complete result tables ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series"))
points the same way, with some nuance. On multivariate TAB the Opus
loop’s detector is first on all four range-aware metrics, ahead of every
classical and deep baseline. On univariate TAB it leads the
ranking-oriented ROC metrics, while KMeans is strongest on the precision
metrics, so the two share the top of that field. On the region-based
affiliation F-measure the detector is only mid-field on TAB, a
consequence of emitting sharp novelty peaks rather than the broad
predicted regions that this measure rewards
(Section [7](#S7 "7. Discussion and limitations ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")).

### 6.2. Did the loop rediscover an existing detector?

The discovered detectors describe each window by a fixed feature vector
and score it by its distance to a model of normal windows, a design that
overlaps with two established families: _frequency-domain_ detectors and
_feature-based_ subsequence detectors. It is therefore fair to ask
whether the loop merely rediscovered a method that already exists. To
test this directly, we compare against the published methods closest to
this design under the identical protocol, each run from its released
implementation
(Table [3](#S6.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 6.2. Did the loop rediscover an existing detector? ‣ 6. Results ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")).
Two are canonical frequency-domain detectors: spectral-residual
saliency ([Ren et al., 2019](#bib.bib41)) and a Fourier-reconstruction
detector ([Rasheed et al., 2009](#bib.bib45)). The others build on
catch22 ([Lubba et al., 2019](#bib.bib43)), the canonical interpretable
time-series feature set, which we use in two forms. The first is
C22MP ([Tafazoli et al., 2023](#bib.bib44)), which scores catch22
features by a matrix profile. The second, our sharpest control, pairs
the catch22 features with our _own_ novelty framework: they are scored
by the same Mahalanobis distance to a Gaussian of normal windows
(“catch22 + Mahalanobis”).

The discovered detector leads all four metrics, and by a wide margin on
the precision-oriented VUS-PR ($`53.9`$ versus at most $`35.0`$). The
“catch22 + Mahalanobis” control is the most telling: holding our novelty
framework fixed and substituting the canonical catch22 features for the
loop’s spectral-organization signature drops VUS-PR from $`53.9`$ to
$`28.4`$. The advantage therefore comes from the particular descriptor
the loop assembled, not from the feature-based-novelty framework alone;
and the discovered detector also clearly outperforms both canonical
frequency-domain detectors and the published catch22-based C22MP.
Extending these univariate methods to the multivariate families by
scoring each channel independently leaves the ordering unchanged, with
the discovered multivariate detector ahead on VUS-PR
(Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Closest-method comparison on multivariate families ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")).

Every ingredient the loop used is individually well established:
sliding-window spectral features, a Mahalanobis distance to a Gaussian
of normal windows, and multi-scale fusion. Each of the methods above
draws on some of them. Yet none combines them as the discovered detector
does, and the discovered combination measurably outperforms each of the
closest existing methods. We read this as evidence that the loop did not
simply rediscover an existing detector, but instead composed known
concepts into a new, and better, one.

| Method                                                   | Aff-F $`\uparrow`$ | F1-T $`\uparrow`$ | Std-F1 $`\uparrow`$ | VUS-PR $`\uparrow`$ |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ | ----------------- | ------------------- | ------------------- |
| Opus 4.8 Loop (ours)                                     | 84.89              | 47.89             | 45.77               | 53.86               |
| FFT detector ([Rasheed et al., 2009](#bib.bib45))        | 78.34              | 27.01             | 26.95               | 35.00               |
| Spectral Residual ([Ren et al., 2019](#bib.bib41))       | 83.52              | 41.01             | 36.44               | 34.75               |
| C22MP ([Tafazoli et al., 2023](#bib.bib44))              | 77.88              | 26.32             | 24.32               | 32.01               |
| catch22 + Mahalanobis ([Lubba et al., 2019](#bib.bib43)) | 75.40              | 22.96             | 21.34               | 28.36               |

Table 3. Comparison with the closest published methods on the TSB-AD
univariate families (Time-RCD protocol; dataset-mean, higher is better
$`\uparrow`$). Each baseline is run from its released implementation and
rows are ordered by VUS-PR; “catch22 + Mahalanobis” keeps our novelty
framework and only substitutes the catch22 feature set for the
discovered spectral signature. Best per column in bold.

### 6.3. Efficiency

Because each detector uses no GPU and trains no neural network, its cost
is predictable and modest.
Table [4](#S6.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 6.3. Efficiency ‣ 6. Results ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")
reports prediction-only wall-clock under the Time-RCD TSB-AD protocol:
we time only each detector’s scoring call, excluding data loading and
metric computation. Our detectors and the classical baselines run on a
single CPU core. The foundation model Time-RCD and the deep detectors,
marked ^(∗), run on a V100 GPU and are timed as deployed: Time-RCD at
inference from its pretrained checkpoint, the deep detectors including
their per-series fit. Our detector is the fastest CPU method in both
regimes and the fastest method overall on multivariate. On the
univariate families it scores about $`5\,\mu`$s per step, on par with
LOF and $`3`$–$`16\times`$ faster than the other classical baselines.
Only Time-RCD is faster, and only because a pretrained transformer runs
a single batched GPU forward pass, whereas every per-series-trained deep
detector is $`40`$–$`120\times`$ slower than our detector even on the
GPU. On the multivariate families our detector leads every method:
Time-RCD costs about $`1.9`$ s per series and the deep detectors
$`2.5`$–$`7`$ s, all on a GPU and all one to two orders of magnitude
slower than our CPU-only program, whose classical subsequence
competitors also slow steeply on the $`25`$–$`66`$-channel series. In
short, the discovered detectors combine their accuracy with runtime and
memory that are easy to reason about, as short auditable programs rather
than models with GPU-scale cost.

### 6.4. Ablation: the model and the search procedure

Holding the harness, the seed program, and the single-principle prompt
fixed, the four searches differ only in the driving model and the search
procedure, which lets us gauge how much each contributes.
Table [7](#A5.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Appendix E Complete result tables ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")
compares the four discovered variants on TSB-AD, and
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Complete result tables ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")
reports the same four in the full TAB field.

#### The driving model matters most

The Opus 4.8 loop is the strongest search overall, and by a wide margin
in the univariate regime, where it leads the other three on every metric
while the other loops (GPT 5.6 Terra and MiniMax-2.5) and the
evolutionary baseline cluster well below it. On the multivariate
families the strongest searches sit closer together: the GPT loop edges
the Opus loop on TSB-AD, while the Opus loop is clearly ahead on TAB, so
across benchmarks neither is consistently in front.

#### The search procedure matters less, but shapes what gets built

Fixing the model to MiniMax-2.5 and varying only the search procedure
(the agentic loop versus the ShinkaEvolve evolutionary search) gives no
consistent winner on accuracy: neither is reliably ahead of the other
across the two benchmarks and the two regimes
(Table [7](#A5.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Appendix E Complete result tables ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")
and
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Complete result tables ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")),
so the search structure looks like a smaller factor than the driving
model. Where the two procedures pull apart is in the kind of program
they return. The agentic loops stayed close to the single-principle
steer and produced shorter programs built mainly around one idea: the
Opus loop returned two compact, genuinely novel single-principle
detectors
(Section [4](#S4 "4. Methods discovered by the searches ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")),
and even the other loops kept to a single idea, as with the GPT loop’s
univariate detector that scores the local total variation of a window in
training-percentile coordinates, though those programs transferred to
the held-out field far less well, most starkly on univariate. The
ShinkaEvolve search, under the identical prompt asking for one novel
principle and explicitly discouraging the fusion of standard methods,
instead converged in both regimes on a hacky weighted ensemble of
standard methods: several standard signals in the univariate program
(autocorrelation structure, gradient-direction entropy, a local
distribution-divergence statistic, a local-rank score, and the original
z-score signal) and, in the multivariate one, a mix that includes a
Mahalanobis distance, per-channel residuals from predicting each channel
from the others, the z-score, and velocity and acceleration terms. We
suspect this might be caused by how the framework works: the
evolutionary framework often asks to merge different ideas together, and
(by construction) it also presents diverse programs as context at each
evolution step, so incremental additions to an already competitive
program tend to be kept even when they grow a larger, less coherent
ensemble rather than a fresh single principle. A single run per regime
cannot pin down that mechanism, but it is a plausible reason the shared
prompt did not prevent this kind of heuristic accretion. The
evolutionary programs also end up markedly longer and more heavily
hand-tuned than the loops’, the evolutionary search is much slower to
run at several hours per regime against the loops’ roughly one-hour
sessions, and its multivariate ensemble is comparatively slow at
inference on the longest series, unlike the tight runtime budget the
loop’s detectors respect.

## 7. Discussion and limitations

The appeal of letting an agent discover detectors lies not only in the
measured numbers but in the resulting artifact: each detector is a
short, readable program, so its inductive biases are inspectable and its
cost is predictable. This contrasts with opaque trained models and makes
the method easy to audit and to port. It also changes where human effort
goes, from designing the detector to designing the harness, the
synthetic-anomaly generator, and the objective that the agent optimizes
against.

Several caveats apply. First, the detector’s standing depends on the
metric family and the benchmark. On TSB-AD it leads across the reported
metrics. On TAB it dominates the multivariate side but shares the top of
the univariate side with KMeans, which is ahead on the precision metrics
there, and it is only mid-field on the region-based affiliation measure
because it is a sharp scorer rather than a region predictor. Second,
although we evaluate on two independently curated benchmarks, a still
broader study across more benchmarks and dataset families (and
potentially real-world deployment) would be needed to confirm the
generality of the discovered detectors. Third, the synthetic generator
is where prior knowledge about anomalies enters. We tried to keep it
broad and realistic but certain types of anomalies that are not captured
well by the prior might be missed by the discovered detectors. The
generator is also a design choice that could be varied, and we do not
claim that the discovered detectors are optimal for every conceivable
anomaly type. Finally, the discovery has a one-time cost in
language-model queries and compute; our efficiency claims concern the
discovered detector at inference time, not the search that produced it.
Though we do report that the searches could be performed within the 20
USD subscription plans and should therefore be accessible to many
researchers and practitioners.

## 8. Conclusion

We asked whether an LLM-driven autonomous research loop is an effective
tool for _writing_ time-series anomaly detectors. Driven by frontier
models and steered toward short, single-principle programs, the loop
discovered related spectral-Gaussian novelty detectors in the two
regimes: a rich, multi-scale spectral-organization signature for
univariate series, and a joint per-channel band-power model for
multivariate series. On the TSB-AD benchmark these detectors lead the
reported metrics and remain near the top of the broader TAB field. Both
are fully unsupervised, run on a single CPU core with no GPU and no
neural training, and consist of short, readable code that keeps them
cheap and auditable.

## Generative AI usage

The research idea, experimental design, and overall structure of this
paper were conceived and developed by the human authors. LLM agents
performed the implementation of the code with human oversight.
Generative AI tools additionally assisted with drafting and editing the
manuscript text, in every case under human oversight, with all claims,
results, and conclusions verified by the authors.
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")
was produced with a generative image model.

## Appendix A Metric definitions

We summarize the standardized metrics used in the main text; full
definitions are given by the works we cite. All accuracy metrics lie in
$`[0,1]`$ and are higher-is-better.

#### Binarization

Our detectors output only raw per-timestamp scores $`a_{t}`$; we never
threshold them ourselves. The region- and point-based measures that need
a binary prediction obtain it inside the evaluation harness, identically
for every method (ours and the baselines): under the Time-RCD/TSB-AD
protocol of the main text the harness reports each threshold-dependent
metric at its score-optimal operating point (sweeping the score quantile
and keeping the best attainable value), while on TAB the label metrics
are averaged over a fixed grid of contamination ratios. Threshold-free
measures (the AUC and VUS families) use the raw scores $`a_{t}`$
directly.

#### Range-aware AUCs (R-AUC-PR, R-AUC-ROC)

Standard AUC-PR and AUC-ROC treat every timestamp independently and with
equal weight, which understates the quality of detectors on extended
(subsequence) anomalies. The range-aware variants add a tolerance region
around each labeled anomaly so that scores raised near a true event are
credited, and then integrate precision-recall or ROC behavior over that
construction ([Paparrizos et al., 2022](#bib.bib9)).

#### Volume under the surface (VUS-PR, VUS-ROC)

VUS removes the dependence on a single tolerance width by sweeping the
size of the boundary buffer and integrating the resulting family of PR
or ROC curves into a volume ([Paparrizos et al., 2022](#bib.bib9)). This
yields a threshold-free and buffer-width-free summary that is well
suited to subsequence anomalies, and it is the headline metric on the
TSB-AD leaderboard ([Liu and Paparrizos, 2024](#bib.bib7)). We order the
TAB baseline field by VUS-PR for this reason (listing our discovered
detectors first), while reporting the full panel of metrics rather than
any composite of them.

#### Affiliation F-measure (Aff-F)

The affiliation metric is a parameter-free, label-based measure that
pairs predicted anomaly events with ground-truth events and scores their
temporal affiliation, combining an affiliation precision and recall into
an F-measure ([Huet et al., 2022](#bib.bib10)). It applies uniformly to
point and subsequence anomalies. Because it scores predicted _regions_,
threshold-free scorers like ours are evaluated on the binary regions the
harness derives from the raw scores as described above.

#### Point-wise and temporal F1 (Standard-F1, F1-T)

The standard F1 is the point-wise F-measure between the binarized
predictions $`\hat{y}`$ and the ground-truth labels $`y`$, computed
timestamp by timestamp. Writing $`\mathrm{TP}`$, $`\mathrm{FP}`$, and
$`\mathrm{FN}`$ for the timestamp-wise true positives, false positives,
and false negatives, it is the harmonic mean of precision and recall,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (2) |     |

````math
\mathrm{F1}=\frac{2\,\mathrm{TP}}{2\,\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{FN}}=\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(\mathrm{Prec}^{-1}+\mathrm{Rec}^{-1}\bigr)\right)^{-1},
``` |  |

with $`\mathrm{Prec}=\mathrm{TP}/(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP})`$ and
$`\mathrm{Rec}=\mathrm{TP}/(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN})`$. The temporal
F1-T relaxes this with a per-series tolerance around each labeled event,
so a prediction close to a true anomaly is credited without requiring
exact timestamp overlap. Both are reported under the Time-RCD protocol
on TSB-AD ([Lan et al., 2026](#bib.bib47)), with the binary predictions
$`\hat{y}`$ formed inside the harness as described above.

## Appendix B Search configuration

#### Synthetic anomaly generator

The validation slice is the last $`30\%`$ of each series’ training
region (at least $`128`$ steps); synthetic anomalies are injected only
into this slice with a fixed seed. Anomalies are placed as
non-overlapping windows, sampled until a target fraction of the slice is
anomalous (subject to a minimum number of windows and a minimum gap
between them), with each window’s length drawn uniformly from a fixed
range. Each window receives a single anomaly type, drawn uniformly from
a mix that deliberately spans both *magnitude* and *in-range
shape/contextual* families, so that a competitive detector must handle
both; the types reimplement those in the GutenTAG generator ([Wenig et
al., 2022](#bib.bib8)). Each type is intended to imitate a generic
mechanism that occurs in practice: a frozen sensor, a valid shape out of
context, a stretched or misaligned cycle, a burst of noise, a drifting
level. Magnitudes are expressed in units of the channel’s robust
standard deviation $`\sigma`$: a *mean* shift adds
$`\mathcal{U}(0.5,4)\,\sigma`$ with random sign; a *platform* sets the
window to its median $`+\,\mathcal{U}(-3,3)\,\sigma`$; a *trend* adds a
linear ramp of total rise up to $`\mathcal{U}(0.5,4)\,\sigma`$; a
*variance* burst adds Gaussian noise of scale
$`\mathcal{U}(1.5,6)\,\sigma`$; an *extremum* is a single-point spike of
$`\mathcal{U}(6,40)\,\sigma`$; an *amplitude* anomaly rescales the
window’s oscillation about its mean by $`\mathcal{U}(1.5,3)`$ (or its
reciprocal) under a smooth bell envelope; a *discord* splices in a real
subsequence copied from a distant part of the *same* series,
level-aligned to the local median (a real but out-of-context shape); a
*warp* resamples a neighboring stretch into the window (a
stretched/compressed, wrong-period cycle); a *phase* shift circularly
rotates the window by a large fraction of its length (a misaligned
cycle); a *flatline* freezes the window at its starting value (a frozen
sensor); and a *scramble* randomly permutes the window’s samples in time
(its value distribution is unchanged but its local temporal structure is
destroyed). All types except the point extremum label the entire window;
the extremum labels only the spike timestamp. The two regimes use the
following generator configurations, which are the ones used for every
experiment in the paper.

- •
  Univariate. Anomalous fraction $`0.02`$; window lengths
  $`\mathcal{U}[4,220]`$; minimum gap $`32`$; at least $`3`$ windows;
  single-channel. Type mix $`\{`$*discord*, *warp*, *phase*, *flatline*,
  *scramble*, *mean*, *platform*, *extremum*$`\}`$, weighted toward the
  in-range shape/contextual families, which cannot be resolved from
  magnitude alone and therefore keep the objective from being satisfied
  by a threshold on deviation, with level and point types retained for
  coverage.
- •
  Multivariate. Anomalous fraction $`0.05`$; window lengths
  $`\mathcal{U}[8,96]`$; minimum gap $`16`$; at least $`3`$ windows; a
  fraction $`0.25`$ of anomalies are applied *jointly to all channels*
  (the rest to a single random channel), which creates cross-channel
  correlation breaks alongside single-channel events. Type mix
  $`\{`$*mean*, *platform*, *trend*, *extremum*, *amplitude*,
  *variance*, *discord*, *warp*$`\}`$.

## Appendix C Discovered detector configurations

We give the key constants present in the discovered programs; complete
executable implementations appear in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Discovered algorithms ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series").
Both detectors standardize from training-region statistics, slide a
window, derive local spectral features, and score their novelty under a
Gaussian model of normal training windows. The univariate detector uses
robust median/MAD feature scaling and a square-root Mahalanobis score;
the multivariate detector uses per-channel mean/std scaling and a
squared Mahalanobis score.

#### Univariate detector

The window is Hann-tapered; its descriptor concatenates the
spectral-organization signature (spectral entropy, log spectral
flatness, spectral centroid, peak concentration, log energy,
log-power/log-frequency slope, low/high band ratio), a within-window
complexity-collapse term (least-active sub-block variation vs
whole-window variation), and a bank of log-spaced band-powers. The
descriptor enters one shrunk full-covariance ($`0.95`$ full-covariance
weight, shrunk toward a scaled identity) Mahalanobis distance
(Eq. [3](#A3.E3 "In Univariate detector ‣ Appendix C Discovered detector configurations ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")),
so each coordinate is scored conditional on the others. The novelty is
evaluated over a dyadic scale space of window lengths spanning short to
long, and the per-scale scores are fused by a tail-emphasized rank
fusion amplified by a gate on the robust-$`z`$ of a window’s distance
above the normal training-distance tail. The per-series pass runs in
tens of milliseconds on typical series and at most a few seconds on the
longest; the window length adapts to the series, and very long inputs
are strided to bound cost. Formally, writing $`z(x)`$ for the robustly
scaled (median/MAD) descriptor of
Eq. [1](#S4.E1 "In The univariate detector ‣ 4. Methods discovered by the searches ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series"),
the per-scale novelty is the shrunk full-covariance Mahalanobis distance

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (3) |  |
``` math
s_{w}(x)=\sqrt{z(x)^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}^{-1}z(x)},\qquad\hat{\Sigma}=\lambda\,\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}\bigl(z^{\mathrm{tr}}\bigr)+(1-\lambda)I,
``` |  |

with $`\lambda=0.95`$. Per-scale distances are referenced to the
training tail as $`e_{w}`$ and fused over the dyadic scale space
$`\mathcal{W}`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (4) |  |
``` math
a(t)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{W}|}\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}}F_{w}\!\bigl(e_{w}(t)\bigr)^{p}\,\bigl(1+L\,\sigma\bigl(e_{w}(t)-c\bigr)\bigr),
``` |  |

with $`F_{w}`$ the training CDF, $`\sigma`$ the logistic, and
$`(p,L,c)=(6,8,3)`$; the exponent $`p`$ and the gate concentrate score
mass on the extreme tail.

#### Multivariate detector

Window $`W=80`$ (shrunk automatically on short series), a small set of
frequency bands ($`6`$) per channel, all $`C`$ channels stacked into one
descriptor after per-window DC removal and Hann tapering. The normal
training-region descriptors are summarized by their mean and one pooled,
ridge-regularized covariance (the sample covariance plus a small
diagonal ridge $`\eta I`$), and the raw score is the squared Mahalanobis
distance of each window to that Gaussian
(Eq. [6](#A3.E6 "In Multivariate detector ‣ Appendix C Discovered detector configurations ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")).
Windows are strided and their number is hard-capped (a few thousand) so
the strided FFT and the Mahalanobis stay near-linear on series up to
hundreds of thousands of steps and dozens of channels. Formally, each
length-$`L`$ window ($`L=80`$) is reduced to per-channel powers
$`P_{k,c}`$ aggregated into $`n_{b}=6`$ bands, log-compressed and
stacked across channels,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (5) |  |
``` math
\phi_{b,c}=\log\!\Bigl(1+\textstyle\sum_{k\in\mathcal{B}_{b}}P_{k,c}\Bigr),\qquad\phi\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{b}C},
``` |  |

and one Gaussian (mean $`m`$, ridged covariance $`\Sigma`$) fitted to
the normal descriptors gives the squared Mahalanobis score

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (6) |  |
``` math
d(\phi)=(\phi-m)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(\phi-m),\qquad\Sigma=\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}\bigl(\phi^{\mathrm{tr}}\bigr)+\eta I,
``` |  |

with $`\eta=10^{-2}`$. Because $`\Sigma`$ is a *single pooled*
$`n_{b}C\times n_{b}C`$ covariance, its cross-channel off-diagonal
blocks encode the normal spectral coupling, so a window that breaks it
scores high even when every channel is individually in range.

## Appendix D Discovered algorithms

For full transparency we reproduce the complete executable
implementations of the two discovered detectors. They are the programs
evaluated throughout the paper, with only harness edit markers and
nonessential explanatory comments removed. Each is a single
self-contained scoring function with a few small helpers; it reads a
training segment and a test segment of one series and returns a
per-timestamp anomaly score, fitting whatever it needs on the training
region without labels.
Algorithm [1](#LST1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix D Discovered algorithms ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")
is the univariate detector and
Algorithm [2](#LST2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ Appendix D Discovered algorithms ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")
the multivariate detector, both found by the Opus 4.8 loop. The
detectors found by the other three searches (the GPT 5.6 Terra and
MiniMax-2.5 loops and the MiniMax-2.5 ShinkaEvolve baseline, each in
both regimes) are provided in full in the anonymized repository linked
in
Section [4](#S4 "4. Methods discovered by the searches ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series").²²
2
[https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TS-AD_submission-7E42/README.md](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TS-AD_submission-7E42/README.md)

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

1 from \_\_future\_\_ import annotations

2

3 import numpy as np

4

5

6 \_NBANDS = 11 \# log-spaced frequency bands whose log-powers enter the
signature

7 \_TAIL_P = 6.0 \# tail-power sharpening exponent on the per-scale rank
curve

8 \_GATE_C = 3.0 \# train-referenced magnitude gate centre (robust-z of
distance)

9 \_GATE_L = 8.0 \# gate amplification strength (additive 1 + L\*gate)

10 \_SHRINK = 0.95 \# covariance shrinkage toward identity (full-cov
weight)

11

12

13 def \_as_1d(values: np.ndarray) -\> np.ndarray:

14 """Return a 1D float series."""

15 a = np.asarray(values, dtype=np.float64)

16 if a.ndim == 0:

17 return a.reshape(1)

18 if a.ndim == 1:

19 return a

20 return a.reshape(a.shape\[0\], -1)\[:, 0\]

21

22

23 def \_strided(x: np.ndarray, w: int, step: int):

24 """Return windows and their start indices."""

25 n = x.size

26 if n \< w:

27 w = n

28 starts = np.arange(0, n - w + 1, step)

29 if starts.size == 0:

30 starts = np.array(\[0\])

31 idx = starts\[:, None\] + np.arange(w)\[None, :\]

32 return x\[idx\], starts, w

33

34

35 def \_interp_to_points(win_scores: np.ndarray, centers: np.ndarray,
n: int) -\> np.ndarray:

36 """Interpolate window scores to timestamps."""

37 if centers.size == 1:

38 return np.full(n, float(win_scores\[0\]))

39 return np.interp(np.arange(n), centers, win_scores)

40

41

42 def \_train_rank(reference: np.ndarray, values: np.ndarray) -\>
np.ndarray:

43 """Map values to their empirical percentile under a training
reference."""

44 ref = np.sort(np.asarray(reference, dtype=np.float64).reshape(-1))

45 if ref.size == 0:

46 return np.zeros_like(values, dtype=np.float64)

47 return np.searchsorted(ref, values, side="right") / ref.size

48

49

50 def \_spectral_org(win: np.ndarray) -\> np.ndarray:

51 """Return spectral-organization features for each window."""

52 wl = win.shape\[1\]

53 taper = np.hanning(wl) if wl \>= 4 else np.ones(wl)

54 wc = (win - win.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)) \* taper\[None, :\]

55 power = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(wc, axis=1)) \*\* 2

56 power = power\[:, 1:\] + 1e-12

57 nb = power.shape\[1\]

58 if nb == 0:

59 return np.zeros((win.shape\[0\], 8 + \_NBANDS))

60 pn = power / power.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

61

62 entropy = -(pn \* np.log(pn)).sum(axis=1)

63 geo_mean = np.exp(np.log(power).mean(axis=1))

64 ari_mean = power.mean(axis=1)

65 flatness = np.log(geo_mean / ari_mean + 1e-12)

66 freqs = np.arange(1, nb + 1, dtype=np.float64)

67 centroid = (pn \* freqs\[None, :\]).sum(axis=1)

68 concentration = pn.max(axis=1)

69 log_energy = np.log(win.std(axis=1) + 1e-8)

70

71 log_f = np.log(freqs)

72 log_p = np.log(power)

73 log_f0 = log_f - log_f.mean()

74 slope = (log_p \* log_f0\[None, :\]).sum(axis=1) / (log_f0 @ log_f0 +
1e-12)

75

76 half = max(1, nb // 2)

77 low = power\[:, :half\].sum(axis=1)

78 high = power\[:, half:\].sum(axis=1)

79 band_ratio = np.log(low / (high + 1e-12) + 1e-12)

80

81 \# Least-active sub-block relative to whole-window variation.

82 nsub = 4

83 sub = wl // nsub

84 if sub \>= 2:

85 blocks = win\[:, : sub \* nsub\].reshape(win.shape\[0\], nsub, sub)

86 blk_std = blocks.std(axis=2)

87 win_std = win.std(axis=1) + 1e-8

88 collapse = np.log((blk_std.min(axis=1) + 1e-8) / win_std)

89 else:

90 collapse = np.zeros(win.shape\[0\])

91

92 \# Log-spaced normalized AC band powers.

93 edges = np.unique(np.round(np.geomspace(1, nb, \_NBANDS +
1)).astype(int)) - 1

94 edges = edges\[(edges \>= 0) & (edges \< nb)\]

95 if edges.size \< 1:

96 band_feats = np.zeros((win.shape\[0\], \_NBANDS))

97 else:

98 band = np.add.reduceat(pn, edges, axis=1)

99 band_feats = np.log(band + 1e-6)

100 if band_feats.shape\[1\] \< \_NBANDS:

101 pad = np.zeros((win.shape\[0\], \_NBANDS - band_feats.shape\[1\]))

102 band_feats = np.concatenate(\[band_feats, pad\], axis=1)

103 else:

104 band_feats = band_feats\[:, :\_NBANDS\]

105

106 core = np.stack(

107 \[entropy, flatness, centroid, concentration, log_energy, slope,

108 band_ratio, collapse\],

109 axis=1,

110 )

111 return np.concatenate(\[core, band_feats\], axis=1)

112

113

114 def \_novelty_curve(train: np.ndarray, test: np.ndarray, w: int,
n_tr: int, n_te: int):

115 """Return train/test spectral-novelty curves at scale ‘‘w‘‘."""

116 w = int(min(w, n_tr))

117 if w \< 6:

118 return None, None

119 \# Bound window count at fine scales.

120 step = max(2, w // 6)

121

122 tr_win, tr_starts, w = \_strided(train, w, step)

123 \# Preserve the training-selected descriptor for short test batches.

124 test_work = test if n_te \>= w else np.pad(test, (0, w - n_te),
mode="edge")

125 te_win, te_starts, \_ = \_strided(test_work, w, step)

126 d_tr = \_spectral_org(tr_win)

127 d_te = \_spectral_org(te_win)

128

129 \# Robust feature scaling.

130 med = np.median(d_tr, axis=0)

131 mad = np.median(np.abs(d_tr - med), axis=0) \* 1.4826 + 1e-8

132 z_tr = (d_tr - med) / mad

133 z_te = (d_te - med) / mad

134

135 \# Shrunk full-covariance Mahalanobis novelty.

136 if z_tr.shape\[0\] \> z_tr.shape\[1\]:

137 cov = np.cov(z_tr.T)

138 else:

139 cov = np.eye(z_tr.shape\[1\])

140 cov = \_SHRINK \* cov + (1.0 - \_SHRINK) \* np.eye(cov.shape\[0\])

141 cov_inv = np.linalg.pinv(cov)

142

143 s_tr = np.sqrt(np.einsum("ij,jk,ik-\>i", z_tr, cov_inv,
z_tr).clip(0))

144 s_te = np.sqrt(np.einsum("ij,jk,ik-\>i", z_te, cov_inv,
z_te).clip(0))

145

146 \# Express distance relative to the training-distance distribution.

147 d_med = np.median(s_tr)

148 d_mad = np.median(np.abs(s_tr - d_med)) \* 1.4826 + 1e-8

149 e_tr = (s_tr - d_med) / d_mad

150 e_te = (s_te - d_med) / d_mad

151

152 tr_curve = \_interp_to_points(e_tr, tr_starts + w // 2, n_tr)

153 te_curve = \_interp_to_points(e_te, te_starts + w // 2, n_te)

154 return tr_curve, te_curve

155

156

157 def detect_anomaly_outputs(train_values: np.ndarray, test_values:
np.ndarray) -\> dict:

158 train = \_as_1d(train_values)

159 test = \_as_1d(test_values)

160 n_tr, n_te = train.size, test.size

161

162 \# Tiny-series fallback.

163 if n_tr \< 24 or n_te \< 12:

164 center = np.median(train) if n_tr else 0.0

165 scale = np.median(np.abs(train - center)) \* 1.4826 + 1e-8 if n_tr
else 1.0

166 tr_scores = np.abs((train - center) / scale)

167 te_scores = np.abs((test - center) / scale)

168 return {

169 "train_scores": tr_scores.astype(np.float64),

170 "test_scores": te_scores.astype(np.float64),

171 }

172

173 \# Multi-scale window lengths.

174 base = int(np.clip(n_tr // 10, 24, 96))

175 base = min(base, n_tr)

176 scales = sorted({

177 6,

178 10,

179 max(16, base // 4),

180 max(16, base // 2),

181 base,

182 min(200, base \* 2),

183 min(300, base \* 4),

184 })

185

186 tr_acc = np.zeros(n_tr)

187 te_acc = np.zeros(n_te)

188 used = 0

189 for w in scales:

190 tr_curve, te_curve = \_novelty_curve(train, test, w, n_tr, n_te)

191 if te_curve is None:

192 continue

193 \# Tail-emphasized, train-referenced rank fusion.

194 tr_g = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-(tr_curve - \_GATE_C)))

195 te_g = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-(te_curve - \_GATE_C)))

196 tr_acc += (\_train_rank(tr_curve, tr_curve) \*\* \_TAIL_P) \* (1.0 +
\_GATE_L \* tr_g)

197 te_acc += (\_train_rank(tr_curve, te_curve) \*\* \_TAIL_P) \* (1.0 +
\_GATE_L \* te_g)

198 used += 1

199

200 if used == 0:

201 center = np.median(train)

202 tr_acc = np.abs(train - center)

203 te_acc = np.abs(test - center)

204 else:

205 tr_acc /= used

206 te_acc /= used

207 \# Light temporal smoothing.

208 span = max(3, base // 8)

209 kernel = np.ones(span) / span

210 tr_acc = np.convolve(tr_acc, kernel, mode="same")

211 te_acc = np.convolve(te_acc, kernel, mode="same")

212

213 return {

214 "train_scores": tr_acc.astype(np.float64),

215 "test_scores": te_acc.astype(np.float64),

216 }

Algorithm 1: The Opus loop’s univariate detector.

1 from \_\_future\_\_ import annotations

2

3 import numpy as np

4

5

6 \# Cross-channel spectral-coherence novelty via joint band-power
Mahalanobis score.

7 from numpy.lib.stride_tricks import as_strided

8

9

10 def \_as_2d(values: np.ndarray) -\> np.ndarray:

11 """Return a float array shaped (time, channels)."""

12 array = np.asarray(values, dtype=np.float64)

13 if array.ndim == 0:

14 return array.reshape(1, 1)

15 if array.ndim == 1:

16 return array\[:, None\]

17 return array.reshape(array.shape\[0\], -1)

18

19

20 def detect_anomaly_outputs(train_values: np.ndarray, test_values:
np.ndarray) -\> dict:

21 train = \_as_2d(train_values)

22 test = \_as_2d(test_values)

23

24 \# Train-region channel standardization.

25 mu = train.mean(axis=0)

26 sd = train.std(axis=0)

27 sd = np.where(sd \> 1e-8, sd, 1.0)

28 trn = (train - mu) / sd

29 ten = (test - mu) / sd

30 C = trn.shape\[1\]

31

32 \# Window length and band count.

33 L = 80

34 L = min(L, max(8, trn.shape\[0\] // 4))

35 nb = 6

36 win = np.hanning(L)\[:, None\]

37 edges = np.linspace(0, L // 2 + 1, nb + 1).astype(int)

38

39 def bandpower(x: np.ndarray, stride: int):

40 """Return per-window, per-channel log band powers."""

41 T = x.shape\[0\]

42 s0, s1 = x.strides

43 n = (T - L) // stride + 1

44 if n \<= 0:

45 return np.zeros((1, nb \* C)), np.array(\[min(L // 2, T - 1)\])

46 starts = np.arange(n) \* stride

47 wins = as_strided(x, shape=(n, L, C), strides=(s0 \* stride, s0,
s1)).copy()

48 wins -= wins.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)

49 wins \*= win

50 F = np.fft.rfft(wins, axis=1)

51 P = F.real \*\* 2 + F.imag \*\* 2

52 feats = np.add.reduceat(P, edges\[:-1\], axis=1)

53 feats = np.log1p(feats).reshape(n, nb \* C)

54 return feats, starts + L // 2

55

56 \# Bound windows for near-linear runtime.

57 MAXW = 4000

58 te_stride = L // 4

59 tr_stride = max(L // 2, int(np.ceil(trn.shape\[0\] / MAXW)))

60 Ftr, \_ = bandpower(trn, tr_stride)

61 Fte, ctr_te = bandpower(ten, te_stride)

62

63 \# Joint model of normal band-power vectors.

64 m = Ftr.mean(axis=0)

65 Sig = np.cov(Ftr, rowvar=False)

66 Sig = np.atleast_2d(Sig) + 1e-2 \* np.eye(Ftr.shape\[1\])

67

68 def maha(F: np.ndarray) -\> np.ndarray:

69 Z = F - m

70 try:

71 Lc = np.linalg.cholesky(Sig)

72 Y = np.linalg.solve(Lc, Z.T).T

73 return np.sum(Y \* Y, axis=1)

74 except np.linalg.LinAlgError:

75 return np.einsum(’ti,ij,tj-\>t’, Z, np.linalg.pinv(Sig), Z)

76

77 d_te = maha(Fte)

78

79 test_scores = np.interp(np.arange(ten.shape\[0\]), ctr_te, d_te,

80 left=d_te\[0\] if d_te.size else 0.0,

81 right=d_te\[-1\] if d_te.size else 0.0)

82 \# Required by the interface only.

83 train_scores = np.zeros(trn.shape\[0\])

84

85 return {

86 "train_scores": train_scores.astype(np.float64),

87 "test_scores": test_scores.astype(np.float64),

88 }

Algorithm 2: The Opus loop’s multivariate detector.

## Appendix F Closest-method comparison on multivariate families

The frequency-domain and feature-based detectors compared in
Section [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2. Did the loop rediscover an existing detector? ‣ 6. Results ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")
are univariate by construction. For completeness we also apply them to
the multivariate families by scoring each channel independently and
averaging the per-channel scores (catch22 features are likewise computed
per channel).
Table [8](#A6.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix F Closest-method comparison on multivariate families ‣ Have an LLM Write Your Anomaly Detector: Autonomous Discovery of Compact, Interpretable Detectors for Time Series")
reports this extension: the discovered multivariate detector remains
ahead on all four metrics, most clearly on VUS-PR. Because these are
univariate methods applied per channel rather than native multivariate
detectors, we treat the comparison as indicative.

| Method | Aff-F $`\uparrow`$ | F1-T $`\uparrow`$ | Std-F1 $`\uparrow`$ | VUS-PR $`\uparrow`$ |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Opus 4.8 Loop (ours) | 85.79 | 49.93 | 46.62 | 35.16 |
| Spectral Residual ([Ren et al., 2019](#bib.bib41)) | 84.17 | 36.32 | 36.12 | 27.33 |
| C22MP ([Tafazoli et al., 2023](#bib.bib44)) | 75.46 | 33.18 | 29.09 | 18.27 |
| FFT detector ([Rasheed et al., 2009](#bib.bib45)) | 77.24 | 29.83 | 28.34 | 17.05 |
| catch22 + Mahalanobis ([Lubba et al., 2019](#bib.bib43)) | 75.73 | 31.81 | 27.15 | 15.82 |

Table 8. Comparison with the closest published methods on the TSB-AD
multivariate families, applying each univariate baseline per channel and
averaging (Time-RCD protocol; dataset-mean, higher is better
````
